stories.bridge: 1947's sliver of germanium became the trillion-transistor chip. Now let's learn the hardware you'll actually touch — from the silicon up.

figures.name: William Shockley
figures.role: Led the Bell Labs solid-state group

stories.hook: On December 16, 1947, in Murray Hill, New Jersey, three men showed their bosses a sliver of germanium that amplified a signal.
stories.narrative: John Bardeen and Walter Brattain had been trying to build a semiconductor amplifier for months under the direction of William Shockley, in Bell Labs' solid-state group — a wartime-born effort to replace the fragile, power-hungry vacuum tube. That December afternoon, with a plastic triangle, a sliver of germanium, and two gold contacts pressed almost touching, they got voltage gain: the point-contact transistor worked. They demonstrated it to executives on December 23; Bell Labs announced it publicly on June 30, 1948, to a famously muted reception — the New York Times buried the story on page 46. The transistor did to the vacuum tube what the tube had done to the relay: it was smaller, cooler, more reliable, and eventually unimaginably cheaper. Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics; Bardeen would win a second Nobel in 1972 for superconductivity, the only person with two physics prizes. Shockley went on to found the company that seeded Silicon Valley — and to a darker later history the industry prefers to footnote. The point-contact device was quickly superseded by the junction transistor and then Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce's integrated circuit (1958–59), but the lineage is direct: every chip you'll handle in this module, every server you'll rack, is that germanium sliver compounded sixty years. When you seat a CPU, you're holding 1947. Treat it with the respect the Times didn't. The Times buried the announcement on page 46 — the editors couldn't know the sliver of germanium would matter more than anything else in the paper that day. Kilby's integrated circuit (1958) and Noyce's planar process (1959) compounded it into the chip; the rest is the digital age. In this module you'll handle the descendants: seat the CPU, respect the silicon, and remember that every server you rack is 1947, miniaturized a billionfold.
stories.title: The story behind the transistor
verifiedClaims: Bardeen and Brattain demonstrated the point-contact transistor December 16–23, 1947
The trio won the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics

stories.bridge: DNS is the phone book you query a hundred times a day. Now let's learn to run it — zones, records, and the troubleshooting that keeps names resolving.

figures.name: Elizabeth Feinler
figures.role: Ran the NIC that maintained HOSTS.TXT

stories.hook: In 1983, Paul Mockapetris looked at the internet's host file — one text file, maintained by hand — and replaced it with a database.
stories.narrative: Before DNS, the internet's names lived in HOSTS.TXT, a single file maintained by Elizabeth Feinler's Network Information Center at SRI: when your machine joined the network, you emailed the NIC, and they added your name by hand. It worked when the network had hundreds of hosts. By 1983 it was collapsing — the file was huge, updates took days, and every machine needed the whole thing. Mockapetris, at USC's Information Sciences Institute, designed the replacement: the Domain Name System, specified in RFC 882 and 883 in November 1983. The ideas were beautifully distributed: a hierarchical namespace (no central file), delegated authority (each zone manages its own names), and caching (ask once, remember the answer). Jon Postel's team implemented it, the root servers were established, and the hand-maintained file retired. DNS became the internet's most-queried database — and its most attacked, from cache poisoning (Kaminsky, 2008) to hijacking, which is why this module teaches it as both infrastructure and battleground. Every nslookup you'll run, every zone you'll configure on Windows Server, is the 1983 design working: distributed, delegated, cached. Mockapetris replaced a text file with a protocol, and the protocol scaled to billions of names. When DNS breaks, everything breaks — which is why the infrastructure specialist learns it cold. Feinler's NIC ran on human labor — emails, phone calls, a text file — and Mockapetris's genius was seeing that names needed a protocol, not a clerk. The hierarchy he designed delegated authority the way the internet delegates everything: no center, just agreements. Kaminsky's 2008 cache-poisoning revelation showed the design's age, and DNSSEC has been the slow fix. In this module you'll run DNS as infrastructure and defend it as a target — the 1983 protocol, still resolving, still under attack. The 1983 protocol, still resolving, still under attack — learn it cold.
stories.title: The story behind DNS
verifiedClaims: HOSTS.TXT was hand-maintained by Feinler's NIC at SRI
Mockapetris specified DNS in RFC 882/883, November 1983
The design is hierarchical, delegated, and cached

stories.bridge: The Ghana story is why this module exists: backups are not IT hygiene, they're the business. Now let's learn backup and disaster recovery like lives depend on it — because they do.
stories.hook: On June 27, 2017, the world's largest shipping company lost its entire network — and was saved by a power outage in Ghana.
stories.narrative: NotPetya arrived disguised as ransomware but built as a wiper: it spread via a compromised Ukrainian tax software update, encrypted machines irreversibly, and tore through multinational networks in hours. At Maersk, the Danish shipping giant, it was catastrophic — some 4,000 servers, 45,000 PCs, and 2,500 applications encrypted. The company's entire Active Directory, the authentication backbone, was gone. Ten days of rebuilding followed, during which the world's largest container shipper ran on paper and WhatsApp. The rescue came from an unlikely place: a domain controller in Ghana that had been offline during the attack — knocked out by a local power cut — and therefore still held a clean copy of the directory. Engineers flew the server's data to rebuild from, and Maersk clawed its way back, at a cost estimated around $300 million. The lessons, reported in detail by Wired's Andy Greenberg, are the curriculum of this module: backups must be offline or immutable (NotPetya ate the connected ones), Active Directory is the keys to the kingdom (protect it like it), and recovery must be rehearsed (Maersk rebuilt in ten days because people knew what to do). Every backup strategy you'll design here — 3-2-1, air gaps, tested restores — is the Ghana lesson generalized. The power cut nobody planned saved the company nobody could afford to lose. Plan your outages; don't wait for Ghana. Greenberg's reporting made the Ghana detail immortal: the domain controller survived because a power cut took it offline at the right hour — luck, not planning, saved the rebuild. The module's lesson is to replace luck with design: offline backups, immutable copies, rehearsed restores. NotPetya didn't care about Maersk's plans; the Ghana server didn't need them. Build so you don't need luck. Replace luck with design: offline, immutable, rehearsed.  Drill restores until they're reflex, not runbooks.
stories.title: The story behind the backup that saved Maersk
verifiedClaims: NotPetya struck June 27, 2017; Maersk lost ~4,000 servers and 45,000 PCs
An offline domain controller in Ghana enabled the rebuild
Recovery took about ten days at ~$300M cost

stories.bridge: 1967's fiction became the cloud's foundation. Now let's learn virtualization hands-on — Hyper-V deep dives start where IBM's imagination left off.
stories.hook: In 1967, IBM built a machine that pretended to be many machines — and the cloud was born, thirty years early.
stories.narrative: IBM's CP-40, built for the System/360 Model 40, ran a control program that gave each user the illusion of their own complete computer — virtual machines, in the term the project coined. CP/CMS evolved into VM/370 in 1972, and for a decade virtualization was mainframe orthodoxy: many virtual computers on one real one, isolated and efficient. Then the PC era arrived, and the idea slept — cheap hardware made sharing seem pointless. It woke up in 1998, when Stanford professor Mendel Rosenblum and his students founded VMware to bring virtual machines to the x86 world everyone had declared unvirtualizable. The trick was binary translation — handling the processor's uncooperative instructions in software — and it worked: VMware Workstation (1999) let developers run multiple OSes on a desktop, and ESX Server (2001) put the hypervisor directly on bare metal for the datacenter. Server consolidation followed, then the cloud: every EC2 instance, every Azure VM, is the CP-40's grandchild. The idea IBM shelved as mainframe esoterica became the foundation the entire cloud stands on. In this module you'll go deep on Hyper-V — Microsoft's hypervisor, the one you'll administer in Windows environments — but learn it with 1967 in mind: a virtual machine is a fiction the hardware agrees to believe, and the hypervisor is the agreement. IBM imagined it; VMware productized it; you operate it. Rosenblum's binary-translation trick was deemed impossible by the experts — x86 was "unvirtualizable" — until VMware shipped it and the experts updated their theories. The pattern recurs in infrastructure: the constraint is usually imagination, not physics. In this module you'll administer Hyper-V knowing the lineage — IBM's 1967 fiction, VMware's 1998 product, the cloud's foundation — and the lesson: virtualize boldly, but understand the layer you're standing on. Virtualize boldly; understand the layer you're standing on.
stories.title: The story behind virtualization
verifiedClaims: IBM's CP-40 (1967) pioneered virtual machines; VM/370 followed in 1972
VMware was founded in 1998 by Rosenblum and colleagues
